sm: Albert Mohler begins with last Thursday's unprecedented summit in Shenzhen, China, where the presidents of the United States, Russia and China met together, with no other leaders present. He argues the photographs are the story, since statecraft often comes down to stagecraft. The setting was formal, with a huge round table and Chinese flags behind Xi Jinping as host. Little of substance seemed to happen, which he says is not a failure, because the meeting was about relationships. The leaders issued a statement renewing their determination to avoid nuclear war.

Mohler compares the scene to the World War II meetings of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin, and later Truman, and says Trump sees himself in that tradition. He says Xi gained stature and national pride as host, and Trump wanted the photograph and treats foreign policy as personal relationships. Trump cited nuclear weapons as the reason for including Russia, though Russia is an economic lesser power, and European leaders were unhappy to be left out. Mohler concludes that Putin gained the most, since the summit feeds Russia's sense of lost glory, and he notes a New York Times headline saying the symbolic win went to Putin. The long-term meaning remains unclear.

Mohler turns to the initial public offering of Anthropic, held the same day as the summit. He says it was valued at 1.28 trillion dollars, exceeding the earlier record set by SpaceX. The shares fell on Friday amid a broad stock market sell-off, and it is unclear whether that will continue today. Some think the market is heading into correction territory, while others see a periodic revaluation. He notes that artificial intelligence is driving nearly all net market growth, and that many Anthropic employees became instant billionaires, including founder Dario Amodei.

He observes that Sam Bankman-Fried, now in federal prison, lost out on about 35 billion dollars, because his bankrupt estate sold its Anthropic stake for 1.34 billion. Mohler describes Amodei as a technology fanatic who warns AI could destroy the world, and as tied to effective altruism, which he calls a secular pragmatism that discounts present human need for hypothetical future good. He calls it hubris that Anthropic's leaders think the company could matter more than the United States, citing a Washington Post report that its prospectus suggested revenue could reach the size of the U.S. economy. He closes by noting that mutual funds and retirement accounts mean many ordinary people are exposed to the IPO.
